claims.text: As-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi alloys contain localized nanoscale chemical inhomogeneities or micro-segregation.
The as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi alloys are predominantly single-phase hexagonal.
Localized chemical inhomogeneities produce a broad distribution of local magnetic exchange energies.
The distribution of exchange energies governs the sharp, hysteretic first-order magnetostructural transition in as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi alloys.
A moderate-temperature, short-duration homogenization anneal can reduce micro-segregation in FeMnNiGeSi.
The anneal can reduce chemical heterogeneity without causing substantial grain growth.
Annealing-induced homogenization narrows the distribution of exchange energies.
The anneal dissolves segregated compositional clusters.
Reducing local exchange-interaction variations smooths the magnetostructural transition.
Greater exchange uniformity reduces transformation energy barriers across the microstructure.
Reduced transformation barriers decrease magnetic or magnetocaloric hysteresis.
The annealed material retains a detectable or significant magnetocaloric entropy change.
Annealed samples will have a less abrupt magnetocaloric response than the as-deposited baseline.
Annealed samples will show less hysteresis than the as-deposited baseline during low-field cycling.
Annealing will broaden the temperature interval of the transition slightly.
Annealing will reduce energy loss during magnetocaloric cycling.
The as-deposited baseline has a large, sharp, hysteretic entropy change caused by chemical inhomogeneity and a broad exchange-energy distribution.
The predictions apply only when annealing avoids excessive grain growth and secondary-phase formation.
The magnitudes of the hysteresis and entropy-change responses may depend on annealing temperature, annealing duration, and initial batch heterogeneity.
Comparison of annealed and unannealed controls using magnetic cycling and TEM/EDX can test whether increased chemical uniformity accompanies reduced hysteresis.

contradictions.description: The baseline attributes a sharp transition to a broad exchange-energy distribution, whereas narrowing that distribution is predicted to make the transition less abrupt and broader in temperature. The direction connecting distribution width to transition width is therefore internally inconsistent or at least insufficiently explained.

The falsification rule treats failure of the anneal to improve chemical uniformity as falsification, even though that result would show failure to achieve the intended intervention rather than falsify the proposed relationship between homogenization and hysteresis.
